column5: Lincoln Township School District || General Motors Motion Picture Catalog, 1953-1954. Details various 16mm films availabe to schools and other non-profits for only the cost of shipping. Catalog has entries with plot summaries, whether the film had sound, whether the film was in color, running time, and weight of film. Catalog includes information on how to borrow films for specified dates. Films are organized into the following categories: Safety and Driver Education, How It Works, Behind the Scenes of Industry, Progress - Past and Future, The Human Side of Industry, Home Economics, Sports, General Subjects, and Special Purpose Films. 65 pages

column5: This series is composed of records created or utilized by individual school districts. It is divided into four sub-series. 1. “District Board of Education Records” contains records created or utilized by the boards of education for individual school districts. 2. “School Census Records” contains records of censuses performed at the school district level, 3. “Teachers’ Reports to the Superintendent” are records that document teachers’ names, school names and numbers, subjects taught, programs of study, pupils’ names, ages, attendance and grades, and the condition of school rooms and materials. 4. "Daily Attendance” records are documents created by individual teachers that document student names, classification, attendance, and grades, occasionally.

column5: This collection contains documents from the rural school system of Lyon County, Iowa dating from 1878-1981. The records cover a majority of the rural schools’ histories, but they are not comprehensive: some records were lost before their transfer to the Center for the History of Rural Iowa Education and Culture. The collection material is arranged into four series -- “County Board of Education, 1883-1975”, “Office of the Superintendent, 1881-1981”, “Township, 1878-1960”, and “District and School, 1882-1966” -- which are sub-divided by format. Series 1. “County Board of Education, 1883-1975” contains records that were created by or utilized by the County Board of Education. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1883-1965 consists of County Board of Education Meeting Minutes, County Board of Education Financial Records, Reorganization and Consolidation Records, Maps, Plat Books, and a small History of Lyon County. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1921-1975 contains County Board of Education Meeting Minutes and Maps of school districts. Series 2. “Office of the Superintendent, 1881-1981” contains records that were created by or utilized by the Superintendent’s Office. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1881-1965 consists of Superintendents’ Secretaries’ Annual Reports, Superintendents’ File, Superintendents’ Cash Book, High School Normal Training Records, Teachers’ Examination Record, Record of Teachers’ Certificates, Teacher Contracts, School Officer and Teacher Records, Educational Directories, Superintendents’ Record of Teachers’ Service, Report of Handicapped Persons to the County Superintendent, Pupil Records, Eighth Grade Examination Records, and Seventh Grade Examination Records. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1881-1981 contains a Superintendents’ Record, High School Normal Training Records, Record of Teacher Attendance and Normal Institute, Teachers’ Examination Records, Record of Teacher Certificates, Teacher/Applicant Record, Teacher Contracts, Office Employee Contracts, Teacher Permanent Cumulative Records, School Officer and Teacher Record, Report of Handicapped Persons to the County Superintendent, City School Enrollment Records and Pupil Lists, Pupils’ Permanent Cumulative Reports, Eighth Grade Examination Records, Eighth Grade Recommendation for Promotion, and Seventh Grade Examination Records. Series 3. “Township, 1878-1960” contains records created by or utilized by the Township Board of Education. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1878-1959 consists of Township Board of Education Meeting Minutes, Township Board of Education Secretaries’ Record, and Township Board of Education Treasurers’ Record. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1878-1960 contains Township Board of Education Secretaries’ Record, Township Board of Education Treasurers’ Record, and a List of Townships and Years of Census Records. Series 4. “District and School, 1882-1966” contains records pertaining to individual school and/or districts. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1886-1966 consists of Teachers’ Reports to the Superintendent, District School Censuses, Library Reports, Textbook Records, Daily Attendance Registers, and a History Booklet for Grant Township, School #4. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1882-1966 contains District Board of Education Secretaries’ Record, Room Registers, Teachers’ Reports to the Superintendent, District School Censuses, Preliminary Classification Reports, Daily Attendance Registers, Classification Records, and a History Booklet for Grant Township, School #4. || Boxes 1, 7, 42, and 43 contain and are located with CHRIEC's over-sized material

column5: This collection contains documents from the rural school system of Madison County, Iowa dating from 1899-1990. The records cover a majority of the rural schools’ histories, but they are not comprehensive: some records were lost before their transfer to the Center for the History of Rural Iowa Education and Culture. The collection material is arranged into four series: “County Board of Education, 1901-1961”, “Office of the Superintendent, 1899-1990”, “Township, 1927-1954”, and “District and School, 1920-1959” -- which are sub-divided by format where necessary. Series 1. "County Board of Education, 1901-1961" contains records created and/or utilized by the County Board of Education. This series consists of County Board of Education Financial Records, Reorganization and Consolidation Records, and Plat Maps. Series 2. “Office of the Superintendent, 1899-1990” contains records created and/or utilized by the Office of the Superintendent. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1899-1990 contains Superintendents' Secretaries' Annual Reports, Superintendents' Cash Book, Superintendents' Library Fund Account Record, Payroll Records, High School Normal Training Records, Teachers' Examination Records, Records of Teachers' Certificates, Teachers' Certificate Renewal Record, School Officer and Teacher Record, Educational Directory, Teachers' Record Cards, Enrollment Records, and Eighth Grade Examination Records. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm consists of High School Normal Training Records, Teachers' Examination Records, Records of Teachers' Certificates, Teachers' Certificate Renewal Records, Teachers' Record Cards, Teachers' Cumulative Experience Records, School Officer, Teacher, and Pupil Records, Eighth Grade Examination Records, and High School Admission Certificates. Series 3. “Township, 1927-1954” contains records created and/or utilized by the Township Board of Education. This series consists solely of Township Board of Education Financial Records. Series 4. “District and School, 1920-1959” is composed of records created and/or utilized by individual districts and schools. column5: The Jerry and JoAnn Kramer Collection is composed of records dating from 1883-2006 that concern the history of education in Bennington Township, Black Hawk County, Iowa; primarily Bennington Township, #4. Divided into two series, "Series 1: Bennington #4 Renovation Project" and "Series 2: Rural School Records", the collection provides insight into the past and present uses of rural schools. || As avid promoters of Iowa’s cultural heritage, Jerry and JoAnn Kramer are committed to preserving the state’s history for the enjoyment of future generations. This fact is evidenced by their involvement in the restoration of Bennington Township, #4 in Black Hawk County. In 1997, the Bennington Boosters 4-H Club conceived the idea to restore the one-room schoolhouse, which had been in use from 1890-1955. Along with the Bennington Neighborhood Association, the Booster Club formed a non-profit steering committee that oversaw the process. In 2000, the group received a $5,000 grant from the Historic Resource Development Program and completed the restoration in the same year. Due to the tireless efforts of all involved, Bennington Township, #4 is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The schoolhouse is currently used by volunteers, such as Mr. and Mrs. Kramer, to inform tour groups of Iowa’s rich educational history. Note written by

column5: The Aletha Hutchison (Jacobs) Collection is composed of materials documenting Hutchison's experiences both as a student and as a teacher in the rural school systems of Iowa and Pennsylvania. The collection includes official school records and Hutchison's personal papers providing insight into many facets of rural school life from 1898-1960. || Born in Buchanan County on July 5, 1884, Aletha Hutchison (Jacobs) attended Homer Township, #3 Mitchell before passing the standard Teachers’ Examination in 1902. After obtaining her teachers certificate, Hutchison (Jacobs) embarked on her teaching career, which would span 58 years, 6 Iowa counties, and 2 states. In the state of Iowa, she taught in Benton County (1900-1902), Buchanan County (1902-1907), Black Hawk County (1912-1916), Grundy County (1916-1920), Wright County (1920-1921), and Webster County (1922). Records indicate that by 1922, she had married Elmer W. Hutchison. This event may have been the reason she left Iowa for Pennsylvania in 1922. The Pennsylvania state school system received 38 years of service from Hutchison (Jacobs) until her retirement in 1960. During her time in Pennsylvania, Hutchison (Jacobs) taught in the following schools: Hummelstown High School in Dauphin County (1922-1924) and Reamstown School in East Cocalico Township, Lancaster County (1926-1960). Despite her death in March 1974, the presence of Hutchison (Jacobs) can still be felt on the educational systems of Iowa and Pennsylvania.

column5: Fred W. Cover spent his life in the rural schools of Iowa - as student, then teacher, and, finally, administrator. He attended the Keokuk County Normal Institute, graduating in 1901. Mr. Cover taught in or served as principal of schools in Keokuk, Butler, Iowa, Mahaska, Black Hawk, and Benton Counties. The Fred W. Cover Papers document the professional life of an Iowa rural school teacher from 1898 through 1946. The Papers include photographs, essays written by Cover as a student as well as class notes, Cover's student records, course lists, and grades, contracts, certificates, newspaper clippings, and commencement programs from ceremonies Cover was associated with - either formally or through former students.

Mr. Sherman continues to conduct research and to add to this collection. || A widely recognized expert on country schools and their culture, William L. Sherman, works to promote and preserve country schools by informing the public of their historic importance. Born in Buckeye, Iowa, Mr. Sherman graduated from Grinnell-Newburg High School and the University of Iowa. For over 35 years, Mr. Sherman worked as a publications/public relations specialist for the Iowa State Education Association. Mr. Sherman’s devotion to country schools has provided him the opportunity to address a range of topics concerning rural schools and create a collection of primary and secondary rural school resources. He has edited two books: Tributes to Iowa Teachers and Iowa Country Schools: Landmarks of Learning. In addition, Mr. Sherman serves on the board of the Country School Association of America and is an active member of the Iowa Historic Preservation Alliance, Humanities Iowa Speakers Bureau, and State Historical Society of Iowa Board of Trustees. The Dr. William H. Dreier Collection serves as a testament to his devotion to rural education. The collection is comprised of his publications, research and notes, presentation and class materials, rural school student records, and student surveys of Black Hawk County rural schools conducted in 1950. || Some materials in the William H. column5: Dorothy E. Mason (Perrin) collected a wide range of textbooks used during her time as a student and teacher in Butler County, Iowa. Born on October 32, 1906, to Fred A. Perrin and Elizebeth Schreurs, Dorothy and her sister Esther M. Becker (Perrin) attended Albion Township, #7 Swanton. In 1920, Dorothy graduated and went on to attend New Hartford High School. Following graduation, she enrolled at the Iowa State Teachers College for the 1924-1925 school year. She went on to teach in the New Hartford School District, located in Beaver Township. Many of Dorothy’s textbooks from #7 Swanton were also used by her sister Esther. A 1927 graduate of New Hartford High School, Esther attended Iowa State Teachers College where she received her certificate in 1929. She returned to #7 Swanton where she taught from 1927-1936.

column5: The DeSoto Consolidated School possesses a rich history which donor, and former student, Jim Riley is working to preserve. Originally located in Dallas County, Van Meter Township, the DeSoto Consolidated School opened in 1924 and served the children of DeSoto, Iowa, until its closure in 1961. The Jim Riley Collection on DeSoto Consolidated School consists of Mr. Riley's reference files which are in the process of being compiled into a book-length work. From 2013-2014, Mr. Riley corresponded with former students to obtain highlights and memories of their time at DeSoto Consolidated School. Informational sheets, letters, and emails from participating students, teacher lists, written works, and the 2004 publication "Memories: DeSoto Consolidated School Class of 1954" compose the collection.

column5: This collection contains documents from the rural school system of Lucas County, Iowa dating from 1866-1966. The records cover a majority of the rural schools’ histories, but they are not comprehensive: some records were lost before their transfer to the Center for the History of Rural Iowa Education and Culture. The collection material is arranged into four series -- “County Board of Education, 1951”, “Office of the Superintendent, 1904-1974”, “Township, 1897-1960”, and “District and School, 1873-1966” -- which are sub-divided by format when appropriate. Series 1. “County Board of Education, 1951” contains financial records that were created by or utilized by the County Board of Education. Series 2. “Office of the Superintendent, 1904-1974” contains records that were created by or utilized by the Superintendent’s Office. Sub-Series 1: Physical Records, 1946-1966 consists of Tax and Financial Records. Payroll records are also included. Sub-Series 2: Records on Microfilm, 1904-1974 contains Records of Schools Taught and Teachers' Complete Records. Series 3. “Township, 1897-1960” contains records created by or utilized by the Township Board of Education. Included are Township Board of Education Minutes and Financial Records. Series 4. “District and School, 1873-1966” contains records pertaining to individual school and/or districts. It consists of District Board of Education Meeting Minutes, District Board of Education Financial Records, and District Census records.

column5: This study was organized by the Iowa Association of Private Colleges and Universities, the State Board of Public Instruction, and the State Board of Regents. Its purpose was to reassess each of the Iowan junior colleges’ and Iowan universities’ demographics and how to improve the overall quality of the universities in the state of Iowa. The Board created eight different sub-goals for the study. Separate committees were then assigned: To estimate the size and characteristics of post high school students. (Committee A); To determine the educational needs of post high school students and how to best accommodate them. (Committee B); To determine the areas of research and service which can be used most effectively and efficiently by post high school educational institutions. (Committee C); How to distribute the programs, research and service of post high school. education among the present and future institutions. (Committee D); To determine the facilities needed to accommodate future students and programs. (Committee E); To determine the future staff needs of post high school educational institutions. (Committee F); To discover the best coordination and governance of education beyond high school. (Committee G); and To find methods of financing post high school education. (Committee H). Upon completion of the study, various higher education institutions in Iowa made some changes to their curricula and guiding philosophies. Junior colleges in the state emphasized the integrity of the university and its development and academic freedom. Iowa State University began to offer more majors in scientific fields. The State College of Iowa began to implement more non-teaching programs due to increased enrollment in these areas. || This collection contains the plans, preliminary findings, committee notes, reports, and correspondence from the Iowa Cooperative Study of Post High School Education, which occured from 1965 to 1967. These print documents are a mixture of handwritten, typewritten, official, original, and copied content. Reports include both narrative content and numerical data. Institutions involved in this study were Iowa State University, University of Iowa, State College of Iowa (now the University of Northern Iowa), the Iowa Association of Private Colleges and Universities, the State Department of Public Instruction, and the Board of Regents. Notable State College of Iowa members who contributed to this project were President J. W. Maucker (Chairman) and Dr. Marshall Beard. Once the study was completed it was delivered to the public.

column5: This file consists of one, twenty page pamphlet, dated December 5, 1891. It is noted as issue Number 1, though no other issues in this series are known. Included in the pamphlet are texts of early United States documents including the Mayflower Compact; the constitution of the United Colonies of New England; and Penn's Briefe and Plaine Scheam. It also contains various declarations of rights, such as statements by the Congress of 1765 and 1774, and the Virginia convention of May 1776. It is possible that this pamphlet was put together by President Homer Seerley and Professor Leonard Parish, as a precursor to their book, History and Civil Government of Iowa (1897).

column5: Latham articulated policies, procedures, and announcements in several series of mimeographed communications. In his Administrative Letters series, Latham informed faculty, administrators, the Board of Education, and others about matters of institutional policy such as use of facilities, requisition of supplies and equipment, travel reimbursement, absences, telephone etiquette, student employment, and faculty classification. His Circular Letters series, sent to the faculty, established policy and distributed news: among the matters treated in these letters are student records, placement of chairs in classrooms, accreditation, the Placement Bureau, telephone service, and assemblies. His Special Announcements series usually told about programs and events such as a visiting speaker. His untitled communications combine many of the functions of the named series noted above.

column5: Constantine Curris was born in Lexington, Kentucky, in 1940. He attended the University of Kentucky, where he majored in political science and graduated in 1962. Curris then attended the University of Illinois, earning his master's degree in political science in 1965 before receiving his Ed.D. in higher education from the University of Kentucky. Curris and his wife, Jo, had two children. Curris worked in a variety of higher education administrative positions throughout his career. He first served as vice president and dean of the Midway College (Kentucky) faculty in 1965. Curris became director of academic programs for the West Virginia Board of Education in 1968 before serving as dean of student personnel programs at Marshall University (West Virginia) from 1969-1971. He then spent two years as West Virginia Institute of Technology's vice president and dean of the faculty. In 1973, he was named the president of Murray State University. Curris became president of the University of Northern Iowa in 1983, Curris' goals while leading UNI were "to improve the physical environment of the campus [and] the quality of undergraduate education and student faculty relations." For example, he supported "campus beautification projects," and various buildings were constructed including the business building (later named in his honor), Kamerick Art Building, Roth Apartments, the Center for Energy and Environmental Education, and the Visitor and Information Center. Additionally, under Curris' administration, UNI experienced a rise in enrollment, stronger enrollment requirements, working towards a "comprehensive strategic planning process" for the university as a whole, and a retooling of its General Education program. He also worked "to gain accreditation for business students." Related to this, UNI garnered national attention for its business and education programs. Curris left UNI in 1995 to become president of Clemson University in South Carolina. Outside of his administrative duties, Curris strongly advocated for public higher education and its students, looking at how those fit in the 21st century. He became president of the American Association of State Colleges and Universities in 1999. His professional experiences included membership or leadership roles in: the Kellogg Commission on the Future of State and Land-Grant Universities, the Iowa Board of Economic Development, the Sigma Chi Foundation, and the Iowa Task Force on Teacher Education and Certification. || This relatively small collection contains information about Dr. Curris's information, but little biographical material. column5: The President’s Newsletters for Constantine W. Curris were published between 1985 and 1995. These newsletters were created to provide information on the actions and processes of the Office of the President during these years. The President’s Bulletin was created by UNI President John Joseph Kamerick with the following purposes, as listed in the inaugural Oct. 1, 1970 edition: Provide official policy statements until an updated Faculty Handbook or a policy/procedures book could be written Provide information on various topics When possible, include texts of local, state and national reports affecting education || This collection consists of paper copies of President's Bulletins from the University of Northern Iowa produced from between 1983 and 1995, as well as the Presidential Newsletters written between 1985-1995. The presidential newsletters from 1985-1995 are in the first folder, followed by the 1983-1994 bulletins. There are 31 bulletin folders that exist in chronological order, starting with issue #121 from September 1983 and ending with issue #151 from January, 1994.

column5: President Constantine Curris proclaimed April 23, 1990, as Founders Day at the University of Northern Iowa. Founders Day was organized to celebrate the history of UNI amd involvement by the entire campus community was encouraged. The main events of the day were an All-University Convocation and Presidential reception. Speakers at the Convocation included Dr. William Lang, Vice President Emeritus, President Constantine Curris, and Dr. Nancy Marlin, Vice President and Provost. In addition, a historical photo exhibit and multi-image slide show were created and presented honoring the University. Although Founders Day was designated as Monday, April 23, events were scheduled throughout the preceding weekend. They included a musical concert, a film viewing, and a recognition breakfast. Student organizations and students living in residence halls were encouraged to organize their own celebrations in correlation with the larger University celebration. The members of the Founders Day Committee, appointed by President Curris were Thomas Thompson, chair, Walter DeKock, Saul Diamond, Edward Rutkowski, James Skaine, Melba Widmer, and Noreen Hermansen. The committee also hired a cooperative education student, Lynn Arnold, to work as an intern.

column5: Robert Koob was born in Graettinger, Iowa, in 1941. He attended the State College of Iowa (now UNI), majoring in chemistry and graduating in 1962. Koob then taught math and science in Moville, Iowa, before attending the University of Kansas, where he earned his Ph.D. in chemistry. Koob and his wife, Yvonne, had seven children. Koob joined the North Dakota State University (Fargo, ND) faculty in 1967 as an assistant professor of chemistry. While at NDSU, he also served as the vice president for academic affairs and the university's interim president. From 1990-1995, Koob was the senior vice president and vice president for Academic Affairs at California Polytechnic State University. Koob served as the University of Northern Iowa's president from 1995-2006. While he was at UNI, the university's endowment increased by over 100%, enrollment and graduate numbers "reached record levels; and the number of privately funded scholarships increased. Additionally, UNI "had more students benefit from international experience than any other master's-level university in the United States." Koob retired from the UNI presidency in 2006 and returned to California Polytechnic in 2008 as provost and vice president for Academic Affairs, a position in which he served until his retirement in 2012. || Researchers should note that there is some repetition of subject coverage between the contents of the first four boxes and Boxes 5-7. This collection gives a good picture of President Koob's interest in community service and university outreach.

column5: The materials in Boxes 9-13 show the wide range of public duties and responsibilities in which President Koob was engaged. It is a good place to study the planning that went into events such as the President's Picnic; other public entertainment; and smaller social gatherings. The collection is arranged chronologically, with much more detailed and complete coverage in the later years.President Robert Koob kept an extremely busy schedule that included local, state, and national meetings; state and national conferences; alumni visits; campus celebrations; community presentations, and campus visitors. His staff assisted him in meeting these obligations by creating folders of background information, schedules, maps, and travel plans for many of these events. Box 6 includes texts of speeches and presentations; schedules for fundraising events and activities; and detailed information about the planning and location of the McLeod Center. Material in Box 6 is arranged by category.

column5: Benjamin J. Allen was named the ninth president of the University of Northern Iowa on April 28, 2006, and assumed his duties on June 5, 2006. He received his doctorate and master's degree in economics from the University of Illinois and his bachelor's of science degree in business economics from Indiana University. President Allen was vice president for academic affairs and provost at Iowa State University and was responsible to the president in all aspects of the academic programs at Iowa State. He has the distinction of having been named the first University Distinguished Professor in Business at ISU. Before joining the ISU faculty in 1979, he taught at Washington State University and was a Brookings Economic Policy Fellow in the Office of Transportation Regulatory Policy, U.S. Department of Transportation. He was the Visiting McKinley Professor of Economics and Public Utilities at the University of Illinois in 1986-87 and held the Oren Harris Chair in Transportation at the University of Arkansas during the 1990-91 academic year. In 1999 he was appointed chairperson of the committee for the study of Freight Capacity for the Next Century, Transportation Research Board, National Research Council, National Academy of Sciences. In 2007, President Allen was appointed by two state college associations (the American Association of State Colleges and Universities and the National Association of State Universities and Land-Grant Colleges) to the Presidential Advisory Committee for the National Commission of University Accountability. In June 2010, President Allen received a Congressional appointment to serve on the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI). This committee is required by law to advise the Secretary of Education with respect to establishment and enforcement of the standards of accrediting agencies or associations. Under his leadership, the University of Northern Iowa has established priorities of increasing student achievement in undergraduate programs and providing statewide leadership in Pre-K through 12 education, including UNI's lead role in the Iowa Mathematics and Science Education Partnership with Iowa State University and the University of Iowa. In July 2011, Gov. Branstad and Lt. Gov. Reynolds declared Science, Technology, Engineering and Math (STEM) a priority for our state. Governor Branstad has asked President Allen to serve as co-chair with Lieutenant Governor Reynolds of the STEM Advisory Council. President Allen also co-chairs the Iowa Business Council's Education Excellence in Iowa Roundtable, a non-partisan forum of business and education leaders focused on improving pre-K-16 academic achievement and establishing career development opportunities. He previously co-chaired the Institute for Tomorrow's Workforce, a non-profit educational foundation helping Iowa learners prepare for the global marketplace. A strong supporter of the local community, President Allen is a member of the executive committee of the Greater Cedar Valley Alliance. He and Pat Allen served as co-chairs of the 2010 Cedar Valley United Way Campaign. || This collection consists of speeches, addresses, and remarks by University of Northern Iowa President Benjamin Allen. In a few cases the entire text is present. However, in most cases there is only a detailed outline or a series of talking points. If the occasion for the speech is a building dedication or other formal occasion, the program for that occasion usually accompanies the speech outline. In a few cases, a CD relating to the occasion is present. A few folders contain only an event program and no text. This collection is an excellent resource for researchers who wish to study what the University of Northern Iowa considered to be the most important matters that it wished to bring to public attention at particular points in time. That is, as the leading spokesman for the university, President Allen emphasized issues that he believed were critical to the university's present and future situation. A few speeches reveal a more personal side of President Allen.

column5: In 2012 Malcolm Price Laboratory School was closed. It was later razed. || Following University of Northern Iowa President Benjamin Allen's announcement of the closing of the Malcolm Price Laboratory School and the University Museum, the Waterloo Courier, the Cedar Rapids Gazette, and television station KCRG, requested and received, under open records laws, electronic mail relating to the closings. The electronic mail, about 2200 pages, covers the period from December 1, 2011 through March 7, 2012. The Waterloo Courier printed several articles relating to the electronic mail release, including an article on April 1, 2012, which is included at the head of this collection. The Courier made the electronic mail available in pdf format on its Web site. The mail was divided into six folders: one folder each for University President Benjamin Allen, Provost Gloria Gibson, Dean of the College of Education Dwight Watson, and the University Museum, as well two smaller folders apparently edited to provide easy access by Courier readers. The Rod Library Information Technologies Department downloaded the files. The Special Collections and University Archives Division printed them out. The printouts are arranged as they appeared in the pdf folders. This collection offers a perspective on the thoughts and considerations of university administrators as they came to their decisions. It also provides a look at campus and community reactions to those decisions.

column5: This collection was assembled in preparation for a re-accreditation visit to the University of Northern Iowa by the North Central Association, Higher Learning Commission in November 2010. As such, the collection is an excellent snapshot of the programs, services, plans, websites, and policies of the university at that time. In addition, the official university publications included in the collection offer a good look at the way in which the university wished to be viewed by the public and the accreditors. Most of this collection served as a body of evidence and support for the self-study performed in preparation for the visit of the accreditation team. Over half of the collection is arranged as supporting documentation for the footnotes and references in the self-study. Files are labeled and arranged in the order in which footnotes or references appear in the self-study: for example, Chapter 1, footnotes 1-10; Chapter 1, footnotes 11-20; and so on. In most footnotes folders, the actual referenced document is present. In a few cases, there is only a further reference to a source. The collection also includes some freestanding documents that were apparently assembled for the use of the accreditation visitors. There is also a limited amount of evidence of the work of the campus preparation committee itself.

column5: These files document the interest and concerns of the Vice President and Provost in the planning, construction, renovation, and use of campus buildings and spaces. This interest, in keeping with the Provost's primary responsibilities, is focused primarily on academic buildings and their use. The files include correspondence, reports, sketches, and a few photographs relating both to major projects, such as the Gallagher-Bluedorn Performing Arts Center, as well as to minor actions, such as room or space assignments. Most of the files are arranged by the name of the building, facility, or space. However, a portion of the files includes information on general and campus-wide planning. The quantity of information about each building or action varies significantly. Some files relate to proposed projects that did not come to fruition.

column5: In accordance with a recommendation for the University Faculty Senate, Vice President and Provost Nancy Marlin created the Center for the Enhancement of Teaching. G. Roger Sell was hired as Director of the Center. He began work in January 1993. After his arrival, Professor Sell conducted a needs assessment for the Center. He then developed a program of services to meet the needs of faculty who wished to improve and expand their teaching capabilities. The services included seminars, surveys, broad studies of problem areas, guest appearances by notable teachers, short papers on a variety of topics, and studies on many issues involving teaching and learning. The services focused on assisting new faculty, strengthening the Humanities sequence and the Capstone course, and developing faculty teaching capabilities. The Center ended operations when Professor Sell took a position at Southwest Missouri State University in 2002. || These files offer a very good picture of the programs and services offered by the Center for the Enhancement of Teaching. The files include Professor Sell's short papers in the improvement of teaching, documentation of the many programs that the Center offered, and strong collections relating to the Qualities of an Educated Person project and Student Outcomes Assessment.

column5: This small collection documents the Partners in Education program of the Waterloo Community Schools. The mission of the program was "to develop partnerships between the community and schools for the purpose of enhancing the academic and social development of students." This program attempted to foster learning and to expose elementary school children to the possibilities of higher education. In this program, the University of Northern Iowa was a partner with Black Hawk Elementary School. The university maintained this relationship from 1987 through 2005.

column5: The Iowa State Board of Regents created the Committee on Extension Service and Cooperation in October 1962. The Regents later changed the name of that committee to the State Extension and Continuing Education Council. The Council was composed of two members from each of the Iowa Regents universities: the University of Iowa, Iowa State University, and the University of Northern Iowa. The Council reported to the Regents by submitting periodic reports to the Regents Interinstitutional Committee on Educational Coordination. || The series consists of annual reports from 1978-1979 through 1986-1987, a biennial report, 1987-1989, and annual reports, 1989-1990 through 1998-1999.

column5: Classic Upward Bound (CUB) is a program that prepares high school students for success in college. It is funded by both the United States Department of Education and the University of Northern Iowa. CUB's purpose "...is to promote students' awareness of the possibility of furthering their education beyond high school and to help students become more aware of their self-worth, uniqueness, culture, and individual creativity." At UNI, students who have finished 8th grade or in in 9th-11th grades from the Waterloo Community School District may apply for CUB. Two-thirds of program applicants must come from low-income and first-generation college families. Program participants are involved in many activities such as recreational, cultural, and educational opportunities, as well as spending six weeks during the summer at UNI, living in dorms and taking classes to help strengthen their academics. || This collection consists of one invitation to the 2017 Annual Classic Upward Bound Banquet.

column5: This collection of material consists primarily of certificates and diplomas used by the University of Northern Iowa to signify the completion of courses of study. There are also a few diplomas and certificates from other institutions and government agencies. First, there are diplomas and certificates that were actually issued to particular students. Most of these documents drifted into the University Archives one-by-one, or as parts of small alumni collections, over the years. These documents are in Boxes 1 and 5. The collection also includes diplomas and certificates that were never issued. Many of these documents are blank, some are spoiled or defective, and some are signed completely or in part by school authorities. A few have names of particular students entered on them. Perhaps these documents were defective in some way or perhaps these students did not finish their courses of study. There are multiple copies of many of these documents. Some of these documents, especially the early ones, are large and handsome, with calligraphic embellishment. The early documents are also interesting in that they include the signatures of the entire faculty and the governing board of the institution. There is a small collection of diploma cases in Box 4.

The exams were taken each term with Term I being the Fall Term and Term II being the Spring Term. The names are entered by Class A, B, C, etc. within each term. Beginning with the 1886 Fall Term, the exam date for each student was entered as well as remarks related to individual students (county appointing each student, assignment, etc.) Toward the back of the first volume are the enrollment figures for the various terms as well as for the entire year. Indication is made as to whether of not the student had either an undergraduate of a graduate grade card. Starting with the 1907 Summer Term, birth dates are included as well. In the volume dated 1911-1919 are lists of students interviewed in the Fall, 1911 including credits by examination (either passed of failed). Students' names do not seem to follow and logical order. This is true of the volume dated 1919-1945 as well.

column5: Project V.I.P. (Volunteers are Important People) was a student-run organization founded circa 1997 at the University of Northern Iowa. In its early years, it was a collaboration among the Department of Residence, Career Student Services, and the Student Organization Center. Project V.I.P.’s main goal was to “promote volunteerism” among the UNI campus community. Project V.I.P. partnered with the Volunteer Center of Cedar Valley to connect with over 75 non-profit organizations. The Volunteer Fair, coordinated by Project V.I.P. and the Office of Experiential Learning, allowed students, faculty, and staff to interact with volunteer organizations’ representatives and learn about volunteer opportunities in the Cedar Falls and Waterloo area. Project V.I.P. was last mentioned as sponsoring volunteer fairs in 2004. However, as of December 2019, volunteer fairs are still organized at UNI. || This collection dates from 1995-2004 and contains materials primarily related to Project V.I.P.’s administrative and promotional tasks. Included are logistical and planning documents for the 1998 and 2000 volunteer fairs, which consist of checklists, flyers, brochures, registration forms, correspondence, set-up and sign-in sheets, lists of participating non-profits and more. Many of the materials contain handwritten annotations. Also included are Project V.I.P. Coordinator position descriptions and information and year-end reports. Items of note: 1995 proposal to establish a UNI Volunteers are Important People Center 2002 U.S. House of Representatives certificate offering congressional recognition of Project V.I.P.’s work, signed by then-Iowa congressman Jim Nussle. || The collection is arranged chronologically.

column5: This series is a collection of contracts, agreements, leases, and insurance claims relating to the operations of the University of Northern Iowa and its facilities. The series contains information relating to the fires that destroyed Central Hall in 1965 and Old Gilchrist Hall in 1972. There is also documentation of the series of problems relating to the KUNI broadcasting tower in the late 1970s and the installation of equipment in the new Power Plant in 1979-1980. While some files are quite small, many files contain extensive material such as insurance loss claims, correspondence, and legal documentation of contentious issues. The material is arranged in an order very similar to that in which it was received.

column5: Sunset Village and its quonset huts were built in 1946 following the end of World War II, with the main goal to provide housing for veterans and their families. The Iowa State Teachers College (later UNI) “acquired 45 quonset huts from the Regional Federal Public Housing Authority and then expended $40,000 to put in sewer, water, and other utilities.” The quonset huts were shipped from Oregon and were located on Highway 57 across from campus, at the end of College Street. Each hut could accommodate two families and military families were given first priority. The huts were ready for occupants in October 1946 and by Fall 1947, units could accommodate 114 students, with all but 18 reserved for veterans. The village continued to grow, with the possibility of housing 138 families in the 72 quonset and barrack-style huts. Rent initially ranged from $20-$33 per month and later, was $25/month and $40/month. These rates were cheaper than those at South Courts mobile homes and Hillside Courts. According to William Lang, “the quonset huts of Sunset Village provided cheap but substandard housing for veterans’ families…” Indeed, there were a few problems with the quonsets, including inadequate heating and their overall issue as a fire hazard. The university announced in Summer 1970 that the Sunset Village units would be gradually phased out as vacancies occurred. In Fall 1971, with Hillside Courts nearing completion, Sunset Village residents were given the option of moving to the new apartments or staying in Sunset Village until Spring 1972. Sunset Village officially closed in August 1972 after which the university attempted to sell the buildings. Ultimately, only three were sold, with some kept for a number of years as storage space and art studios. The remainder of the buildings were razed. || This collection consists of a 152 page bound notebook, dating from 1946-1948. It consists of entries noting when specific people and their families moved in and/or out; whether the unit was furnished; occasional notes about damage (see page 6); and street names for units, such as E. Navy St., E. Marine St., and E. Army St.

column5: This series seems to be a combination of material accumulated by the Registrar and several chairs of the University Faculty Senate. These files often contain correspondence, committee reports, and other documents associated with particular docket and calendar items. If a researcher wishes to go beyond Senate minutes or announcements to gain a better understanding of an issue under consideration, this series might prove useful. Portions of the files seem to have been created by chairs of the Faculty Senate, such as Professors Myra Boots and John Longnecker. But other portions seem to have been from a time when the Registrar, or a member of the Registrar's staff, served as secretary to the Faculty Senate. The contents and order of each annual file vary.

column5: This series has come to the University of Northern Iowa Archives in many small increments over the years. Files for some years are strong, with associated documents. The records of the General Education Committee consist primarily of material assembled by several of its chairment, including A.E. Brown in the mid-1940s and Edward Amend and Joan Diamond in the 1970s. Since much of hte committee's work was directed toward the production of major reports and program revisions, these committee records contain a large amount of background reading material including brochures about other schools' programs, general studies convention literature, and evaluations of general education courses at UNI. These different forms of information are so completely integrated with routine minutes, correspondence, and heavily annotated preliminary drafts and memoranda that no attempt has been made to sort material into categories. || Material is in a rough chronological arrangement as it came from the chairmen.

column5: The Campanile Committee was responsible for leading fundraising efforts to build the Campanile. The committee also had some responsibilities for Campanile upkeep and improvement after it was built. Among the most important documents in this series are the Fasoldt correspondence and the letter from James Owen Perrine. In the Fasoldt correspondence, Dudley Fasoldt writes at length about the Fasoldt clock mechanism that was originally mounted in the Campanile. J. O. Perrine, in his 1946 letter to I. H. Hart, writes about what he believed to be his pivotal role in the acquisition of the clock mechanism. There are also important exchanges of correspondence between Teachers College officials and the architects of Proudfoot, Bird, and Rawson on the design and construction of the Campanile.

column5: Professor Len Froyen (Class of 1957) and Don Adams (Class of 1957) were co-chairs of a planning committee, which, in cooperation with the Alumni Office, organized a reunion for former residents of Stadium Hall, a men's residence facility located in O. R. Latham Stadium from 1947 through 1961. The planners conducted extensive research and eventually located over seven hundred living former residents. Over one hundred former residents attended the reunion that was held on October 14 and 15, 2005. The 2006 donation included a DVD recording of the reunion program, a directory of Stadium Hall residents, pre- and post-reunion publicity, and correspondence.

column5: This series is a collection of Alumni Association documents developed over the years by Alumni Association staff. It consists of material found in five three-ring binders that were labeled Alumni Books 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Books 1 and 2 were not present. Each binder included material from a particular chronological period, though there was some overlap between binders. Book 3 contained material from 1954 through 1971; Book 4 contained material from 1971 through 1978; Book 5 contained material from 1979 through 1984; Book 6 contained material from 1984 through 1986; Book 7 contained material from 1986 through 1988. The binders contained many kinds of records relating to Alumni Association affairs, including Board minutes, financial reports, articles of incorporation, by-laws, rosters of award winners, committee reports, membership reports, and samples of material mailed to alumni. All material remains in the same order in which it was received.

column5: This series is a collection of Alumni Association reports on UNI alumni who earned advanced academic degrees from 1880 through about 1963; alumni engaged in particular occupations; and alumni sorted by county of residence. In one group of reports, alumni are divided into categories depending on the advanced degrees that they earned, including Ph. D, M. D., D. D. S., D. V. M., D. D.,and J. D. There are also files sorted by occupations, including guidance counselors, school superintendents, coaches, researchers, and collegiate faculty and staff. There is a file of men with master's degrees. Finally, there is a file of alumni arranged by Iowa county of residence. There is biographical information about most of the alumni in these files, including graduating class, occupation, academic degrees, address, and spouse.

column5: The University of Northern Iowa Alumni Association and Rod Library Special Collections & University Archives collaborated to develop Panther Pride: Homecoming 2017 Oral Histories. This project was especially designed to capture memories of the Golden Grads group in 2017. For this project, students and alumni participating in Homecoming 2017 events shared memories from their time on campus and advice to future students. These oral histories were video recorded at Rod Library with the help of the Digital Media Hub staff and students. Recordings originally took place in the Library’s green screen room, but due to noise, the location shifted to the Library’s first floor. || The Panther Pride Oral Histories collection contains access copies 15 mp4 video and audio recordings of oral histories conducted in October 2017 with University of Northern Iowa students and alumni. Preservation recordings also exist in the form of .MOV and .MXF files.

column5: Note to researchers: This filing system code accompanied the collection when it arrived in the University Archives. The individual elements of the code consist of two letters and a number, such as A4A, B6L, or L7B. The code is a hierarchical system that mirrors the administrative organization chart of the university. Many of the folder tabs in this collection included this code. When that code appeared on the original folder, the records processor included the code on the new folder. However, the collection itself was not in anything approaching coded arrangement when it arrived in the Archives. Nor did every folder include a coded notation; many folders were labeled "Miscellaneous". In addition, much of the collection had been developed long after the last revision to the filing system codes. Consequently, the records processor imposed his own order on the collection, though with some reference to the apparent original order. Researchers may wish to consult the 1991 filing guide to get a clearer sense of the contents of some of the folders.

column5: The University of Northern Iowa's Educational Media Center was a campus-wide organization created to facilitate learning through providing faculty with media and equipment to help them in the classroom. The organization created informational booklets beginning in 1949, branched out to create Curriculum Laboratory informational booklets and catalogues in 1959, and started creating multi-media catalogues in 1972. These materials were published until 1992, when the organization became the Center for Educational Technology. || This series is a collection of information booklets about the Curriculum Laboratory’s audio-visual services, multimedia catalogues from the Educational Media Center, and other information booklets about the Educational Media Center, such as the faculty handbook and annual summary. The purpose of the Curriculum Laboratory booklets was to inform people about the audio and visual services located there, and to make students aware that they were welcome to use those services. The multimedia catalogues include the collection of tapes, film, and other forms of media available for checkout at the Curriculum Laboratory; an index of the titles of those pieces in the media collection and their producers. || This collection is arranged chronologically.

column5: The Board of Student Publications, as it was originally called, has had a variety of names over the years. It was renamed the Board of Control of Student Publications in the 1934-1935 school year before reverting to the Board of Student Publications during the 1935-1936 academic year. In 1936-1937, it became the Board of Control. The next documented minutes are from the 1948-1949 school year, when the organization was called the Board of Control of Student Publications. In 1972-1973 the name was changed again to the Board of Student Publications. || The school years 1932-1933, where the collection begins, through 1938-1939 are documented only by minutes. There is no documentation for the years 1939-1940 through 1942-1943. Financial records are the organization’s only documentation from 1943-1944 through 1947-1948. After that the documentation is very strong on minutes through 1991-1992. Most years between 1948-1949 and 1961-1962 have financial and personnel documentation. The school year 1961-1962 was the first to retain documents of policies, constitutions, and by-laws. Most years thereafter did, as well. In the 1968-1969 school years documents began to be retained for correspondence, proposals, specifications, recommendations, and requisitions for equipment. From 1968-1969 through 1991-1992 the documentation is strong in each area. Included in the 1982 documents is information from the Associated Collegiate Press and National Council.

column5: The theme of the lantern slides centers on the country school in Iowa during its peak years and the role of the Iowa State Teachers College in the growth of the country school. The 903 glass slides are divided into two categories: The country schools and the Iowa State Teachers College (ISTC). The country schools group is further sub-divided into two series: the lettered series, B-Y, and the miscellaneous series. The lettered series illustrates the general life of the student in the country school room and shows scenes related to the daily functions and activities of the school. This series also includes images of town schools. The miscellaneous series includes photographs of Iowa country school buildings, school transportation, farm scenes, maps indicating schoolhouse locations, and interior photographs of rural schoolrooms. The Iowa State Teachers College group is also sub-divided into two series: the lettered series, A-E, and the miscellaneous series. The lettered series includes images of buildings on the I.S.T.C. campus, athletic scenes, students preparing to become teachers, the Campanile, etc. The miscellaneous series includes photographs of the nursery school at I.S.T.C., songs and cheers, main I.S.T.C. buildings, and portraits of both I.S.T.C. Presidents—Seerley and Latham.

column5: This series consists of printouts of Kudos that appeared online. Kudos was an Office of Public Relations publication which acknowledged those faculty and staff members who had recently or soon would be published; those who recently presented papers, lectures, and exhibitions; and those who won awards and honors. Kudos was first published as a permanent section of the Campus News Network (CNN) newsletter in 1990. At some point the section was expanded to an insert included with the CNN newsletter once or twice a month. In April 1998, the Office of Public Relations began publishing Kudos only online and discontinued the page in 2008. Afterward, the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences (CSBS) continued publishing Kudos in its newsletter, but only for faculty and staff in that department. Special Collections maintains an index to Kudos, which is found in the reading room. Kudos from 1990-March 1998 are indexed with the CNN Kudos from 1998-2008 are included in this box, along with 2009-2016 issues of the CSBS newsletter.

column5: In October 1960, a group of office workers at the Iowa State Teachers College (now the University of Northern Iowa) organized a professional support group called the Clerical Club. The club changed its name several times during its history. It was also known as the UNI Association of Education Secretaries (AES), UNI Association of Office Personnel, and in about 1991, became UNI Association of Educational Office Personnel (AEOP). Some of the major community contributions made by UNI AEOP include annual workshops that provided training sessions for office personnel from around the state; fundraisers, such as Adopt-A-Family Christmas Project for needy families; and scholarships. Due to declining membership, the UNI AEOP dissolved in 2007. || For information on the highlights of the group’s history, see Box 21 Folder 1.

column5: Phi Delta Kappa (PDK) is an international fraternity for people serving in the field of education, as well as both undergraduate and graduate students who are pursuing careers in education. PDK was first established at the Iowa State Teachers College (now the University of Northern Iowa) in 1948 as the Alphi Phi field chapter. In 1957, the campus chapter, Delta Beta, was installed on campus. || The Phi Delta Kappa series dates from 1950 to 2000 and contains information about and by the University of Northern Iowa chapter of Phi Delta Kappa. The majority of the materials are administrative records and photographs. Types of administrative records include chapter history, handbooks, annual / financial reports, correspondence, newsletters, board minutes, rosters, newsletters, by-laws, and more. Also included are conference and council proceedings, some of which contain handwritten notes and annotations. The series also contains many photographs from PDK events, meetings, and more. The photographs date primarily from the 1990s, though there are also a number of undated folders.

column5: The Faculty Dames was a club organized to "promote sociability and friendship among the faculty wives." The club met for the first time on March, 10, 1924. The Faculty Dames changed their name to the University Dames in 1972, and, in 1992, to UNI Connection. Sociability among faculty and faculty spouses is still promoted by UNI Connection. The group also operates a scholarship program for non-traditional students.

column5: This collection consists of master agreements, correspondence, negotiation documents, United Faculty Presidents' notebooks, arbitration records, grievance records, reports, meeting minutes, newsletters, and audio cassette tapes documenting the history of UNI's faculty labor union, United Faculty (UF). Many of these records document the process of negotiating new collective bargaining agreements with the University, including research conducted by UF, proposals, and arbitration proceedings between the Univerisy and UF. Also documented are the non-negotiating activities of the union over the years, such as the constitution and bylaws, promotional materials and FAQs, surveys and reports on working conditions, meeting minutes of the executive board and the board of the Iowa Higher Education Association (IHEA), and administrative papers. Individual grievance and arbitration records are restricted, while those invlolving the union itself are available to researchers. || United Faculty (UF) is a labor union representing faculty at the University of Northern Iowa. Formed in 1975 through a merger between the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and the Iowa Higher Education Association (IHEA), it was elected in 1976 as the sole representative of faculty for purposes of collective bargaining.

column5: The second series, Correspondence, is arranged into two subseries. Types of materials include correspondence, memos, and invoices. The first subseries, General Correspondence & Documents, 1963-1988, contains materials related to budgetary/salary matters; departmental issues, such as conferences, positions, open positions, and graduate assistantships; guest lecturers; discussions of journals/publications and textbooks; College of Business and Behavioral Sciences matters; and topics related to the Middle East. Much of the material is to/from department head Basheer K. Nijim. The second subseries, Administrative Correspondence, 1959-1970; 1981-1982 consists of correspondence pertaining to departmental position openings. Included are letters from various scholars applying or asking about jobs, sometimes with accompanying resumes and references. The subseries is arranged chronologically. Also included in this subseries is a grouping of materials focused specifically on the 1971-1972 search for the College of Business and Behavioral Sciences dean position. This subseries is restricted and closed to researchers.

column5: Series 1, Correspondence, 1957-2009, consists of Gilgen's incoming and outgoing correspondence with various individuals and organizations. Materials include handwritten and typed letters, emails, and postcards. The correspondence covers many subjects, with the bulk concerned with Gilgen's publications and research, ranging from journal articles to book manuscripts. Other letters focus on his time as a Fulbright-Hays lecturer (1971-1972) at University College Galway, including his family's passport photographs; a handful of letters related to joining the UNI faculty in 1973; 50th anniversary materials for Garfield High School's Golden Anniversary (Akron, OH); and early 1990s correspondence concerning the Clinton administration's health care reform efforts in relation to the field of psychology. The majority of this series is business and professional-related with a small amount of personal content. This series is arranged chronologically.

column5: The Administrative Records series is broken up into two categories. The first is comprised of department minutes which include topics such as graduate students; curriculum and courses; committee work; the department's budgets; promotions and tenure; department events; faculty hirings; and departmental student employees. A majority of the minutes are typed, with some containing handwritten annotations. Also included are a few handwritten notes from assorted department meetings. These materials span 1973-1993 and are arranged chronologically by academic year. The second grouping in the Administrative Records series consists of the department's General Correspondence & Documents, ranging from 1985 to 1993. A variety of topics are covered including discussions of courses and curriculum requirements; salary and financial information; administrative and strategic goals for the broader College of Social & Behavioral Sciences; notes from Department Head meetings; reports; a few minutes from the CSBS faculty senate meetings; and schedules/itineraries from the interview process for potential hires. These materials are arranged chronologically by academic year.

column5: This subject file contains material collected during the terms of three different Library Science department heads. Donald Rod was the department head from 1953-1968, Clyde Greve from 1968-1971, and Elizabeth Martin from 1971 until her retirement in 1991. Other faculty members who worked during this period and are mentioned in these papers are Leah Hiland, Mary Lou McGrew, Gerald Hodges, W. Duane Johnson, Arlene Ruthenber, and Charles Adams. Boxes 1-2 consist of material on administrative matters, such as correspondence, meeting minutes, and other departmental business; and the Library Science program, including departmental restructuring, enrollment, and the curriculum. column5: Arranged alphabetically by title, followed by the year of publication. || Dr. Waack donated an extensive collection of sheet music to Special Collections. These range in date from 1892 to 2005, the bulk of which were published in the 1920s and 1940s. The piano/vocal scores consist of popular songs of the times, movie and Broadway show tunes, hymns, patriotic songs from both World Wars, and a few piano pieces in the more classical vein. Because many of the songs were published before Dr. Waack was born, it is believed this music may have been owned by his mother or grandmother.

column5: The collection is wide-ranging. It includes speeches by Deans Roy H. Saigo and Gerald W. Intemann as well as records of several committees in which the Dean of the College of Natural Sciences had a particular interest. There is also good information about some of the early organizational plans for the college administrative structure, shortly after the college was organized. Probably the strongest point of this collection is the material relating to the design, construction, renovation, and use of facilities for departments and programs in the College of Natural Sciences: namely, the Science Building (later McCollum Science Hall), the Industrial Technology Center, Wright Hall, Latham Hall, and the Center for Energy and Environmental Education. Material relating to the original construction of and later additions to McCollum Science Hall is especially detailed. The collection is also strong in documenting the development and early years of the Doctor of Industrial Technology degree in the Department of Industrial Technology. There is also an excellent fifty-year run of correspondence and reports outlining the involvement of the University of Northern Iowa with the Iowa Lakeside Laboratory.

column5: Music has been a subject at the University of Northern Iowa since its founding in 1876. Now part of the College of Humanities and Fine Arts, music was initially offered alongside art in the Art Department. This arrangement lasted until 1892, when the two subject areas split, and music became the Vocal and Instrumental Music Department. This name lasted until 1896, when the department name switched to the broader Music Department. The Music Department experienced fairly frequent name changes in the early 20th century. In 1909, it split into four distinct divisions: the Public School Music Department, Orchestral and Band Music Department, Pianoforte Music Department, and the Voice Department. By 1911, however, there were just two music departments, the Music Department and the Violin, and Orchestral and Band Music Department. Over the next few years, department name changes included the Orchestral Music Department, and shifts between the Music Department to the Public School Music Department, and back again. By 1934, the two different music departments at the time, the Orchestral Music Department and the Music/Public School Music faculty merged to form the single Music Department. The final name change came in 1978, when the department was renamed the School of Music. || This collection consists of School of Music programs for a variety of events including student, studio, and faculty recitals, ensemble concerts, and guest artist performances. It dates from 1985-present. Specific events include All-State, Chimes of Christmas, the Tallcorn Jazz Festival, and the Faculty Artist Showcase. The collection also contains web content captured using the web archiving tool, Archive-It. To view this content, please visit the Concert Program web archive. Represented ensembles include (but are not limited to) Jazz Bands I and III, Jazz Panthers, UNI Chamber Singers, Symphonic Band, Wind Symphony, Concert Band, New Horizons Band, the Symphony Orchestra, UNI Singers, Women's Chorus, and the Varsity Men's Glee Club. || The collection is arranged chronologically by academic year.

column5: The "Songs in the Air" radio program was produced by the Iowa State Teachers College (ISTC) radio studios and began circa 1948, lasting until at least 1958. The fifteen minute program was broadcast every Monday on the WOI Ames radio station. It was conducted by ISTC music professor John Mitchell, with the goal of teaching "rote songs" to Iowa elementary students. ISTC students sometimes participated in the program as studio singers, helping to lead the listeners in singing. In August 1949, ISTC radio director Herbert V. Hake noted that the program "received excellence response" the previous year. Audiences ranged from 15,000-25,000 school children in 88 Iowa counties, roughly 3,000 classrooms, and six surrounding states. The program appealed to rural schools where music classes were not as robust as those in cities. || This collection contains three ISTC "Songs in the Air" study guides. Each contains a number of songs, complete with musical scoring and lyrics, as well as copyright and publishing information for a majority of the songs. Of note is that Herbert Hake provided illustrations for the study guides, including the 1949-1950 guide in this collection.

UNI people are featured in these publications. There is also a newspaper article about Dorothy Grant in which she recounts physical and emotional abuse in her domestic life. In August 1997, additional publications were added to the collection including Universalism in Iowa, The Unitarian Universalist Society of Black Hawk County, and Plant Collecting in Iran. In My Norwegian Heritage, Dorothy Grant outlines her family's genealogy. Also included were six transcripts of talks she gave during the 1992 Centennial of Ruth Suckow, and a biography of Suckow's husband Ferner Nuhn.

column5: Gifford Simeon Robinson was born in Tremont, Illinois, on May 28, 1843. He served in the Civil War, during which he was seriously wounded at the Battle of Chickamauga. After the war he studied law at Washington University in St. Louis, graduating in 1869. He moved to Storm Lake, Iowa, in 1870 and set up a law practice. He was later elected to the Iowa House of Representatives, serving from 1876-1878. From 1882-1886 he was an Iowa state senator, and from 1888-1899 a justice on the Iowa Supreme Court. Three of those years were spent as Chief Justice. After leaving the court he was appointed to the Iowa Board of Control, serving in that capacity from 1900-1913. Mr. Robinson died on his 93rd birthday, May 28, 1936. || This box contains one typewritten letter from G.S. Robinson to Professor David Sands Wright, dated October 24, 1916, in response to Professor Wright's request for information about the early history of Iowa State Normal School.

column5: Series 1, the Charles E. Hearst materials, consists of records created and used by Charles E. Hearst, as well as biographical information and other documents related to the Hearst family as a whole. The materials created by Charles E. Hearst include notes about agricultural issues, records from the Maplehearst family farm, and his work in passing agricultural legislation. The bulk of his records consist of his personal and professional correspondence. Some of this correspondence has been photocopied due to the originals' fragility and deteriorating condition. Most of the correspondence written to and from Hearst were written during his term as the Iowa Farm Bureau president from 1924 to 1935. The correspondence, and his records in general, reflect the range of problems which farms and agriculture faced during the 1920s and 1930s. The correspondence also related to Hearst's work shepherding legislation through the Iowa legislature and United States Congress, including the Mc-Nary Haugen Bill and the Agricultural Adjustment Administration of the New Deal. Other types of materials in the Charles E. Hearst series include news releases, American Farm Bureau Federation circulars, position statements from various agricultural organizations, and ephemeral agricultural publications. The remainder of the Charles E. Hearst series includes a handful of items created by other Hearst family members, photographs of the Hearst family and farm, and news clippings.

column5: The Charles Joseph Hearst and Gladys Henderson Hearst series contains materials related to both Charles Joseph and Gladys. Gladys Henderson Hearst's files consist of documents related to and representative of her time in the Women's Accepted for Voluntary Emergency Service (WAVES) during World War II. Types of materials include papers and photographs. The photographs are a combination of the WAVES training program at the Iowa State Teachers College (now the University of Northern Iowa) and nationally. Many include types and handwritten captions. The Russia trip materials consist of news clippings related to an agricultural exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union in 1955. Charels Joseph Hearst was part of the American delegation that visited the Soviet Union. These materials were likely collected by Charles or Gladys. Note: Charles Joseph Hearst's personal papers are held at Iowa State University.

column5: A major component of James Hearst's papers are the publications included in the collection. Within this grouping are iterations of Hearst's work, such as drafts and published forms. Please note that this is not a complete run of Hearst's work that appeared in this publication type. Also included are publication logs of James Hearst's work. Family members and Hearst himself kept these logs in an attempt to record when where his work was published. The logs represent a record of his publication history.

column5: Unpublished typescript with editorial marks by James Hearst. 178 pages plus 2 pages of story outline. No date. This typescript seems to be a draft of a novel or series of short stories. The assumed title of this typescript, The running of widows, is simply the name given at the top of the first page of the first chapter. The remaining chapters are titled by the name of the character featured in that particular chapter. The first chapter sets the theme for the work: ten widows, of considerably different circumstances, organize themselves into a mutual assistance network. Each of the remaining chapters tells the story of one widow's life. The individual chapters of this typescript seem to be fairly well-developed. And there are relationships and references between and among the chapters. But there does not seem to be a resolution, summary, or conclusion to the collection.

column5: 1. One large set of logs was kept in three 7 inch by 9 inch ring binders. The binders were discarded during the processing of the collection, because they were badly deteriorated. The pages from each binder were then transferred into individual file folders, one folder per binder. Nearly all of the pages in the binders consist of typed copies of James Hearst's poems. But in a few cases, instead of a typed copy of a poem, there is a clipped copy from the original publication, or a photocopy of the original publication, glued to the page. In nearly all cases, there are bibliographic citations to the publication(s) in which a poem appeared, written or typed at the bottom of each page. The overall arrangement of the three binders is chronological, according to the time of the first appearance of a poem in print. However, there are significant departures from this order, especially in folders one and two. The binders also include a few poems that are noted as "unpublished." Meryl Norton Hearst was likely responsible for maintaining this log. column5: James Hearst's correspondence comprises the majority of this series. It contains approximately 1000 incoming and outgoing letters, which are a mix of personal and professional topics and correspondents, such as with Hearst's first and second wives, friends, publishers, discussions about his writing, his employment at the University of Northern Iowa (UNI), and much more. One of Hearst's most frequent correspondents was UNI president James William Maucker, who often signed off his letters as "Bill." Other notable correspondents include Ferner Nuhn, Bess Streeter Aldrich, Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, and Jesse Stuart. Also included are letters from United States Vice President H.A. Wallace; one letter from former First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt to Carmelita Hearst (August 21, 1951); and one letter from Randolph Hearst (May 22, 1974). Some of the correspondence is addressed to Carmelita Hearst, James Hearst's first wife, and Meryl Norton Hearst, his second wife. There are also many letters between Hearst and editors, publishers, and presses discussing his work and publications. There is a name index to most correspondents available in the University Archives and digitally. "T.L.S." means Typed Letter Signed. "A.L.S." means autograph letter signed. column5: This collection was sorted from a much larger collection of memos, correspondence, department meeting minutes, and other files accumulated by a number of School of Business faculty members and sent to SC&UA over many years. His numerous, detailed memos to department faculty and others give a good picture of the history and development of the department. Prominent faculty members mentioned in this collection include Robert Waller, Paul Uselding, Constantine Curris, Peter Goulet, and James Martin.

The collection was likely assembled by Richard Dietl, a member of the State College of Iowa sports information staff, in 1964. This collection offers a good look at preparation for and participation in the bowl game. There is an especially nice selection of photographs of individual players, groups of players, and Coach Stan Sheriff.

column5: This small series was complied by the University of Northern Iowa Sports Information Office and its predecessor offices intermittently over the period of many years. Work on this series seems to have begun in about 1947 and was then updated to a limited extent and on a number of occasions. Sources for information seem to have been the Old Gold, the student newspaper, and other sources. Contents include contest results and individual competitors' statistics. There are also brief lists of letter winners and All-Americans. Coverage varies widely over the years, but seems to be strongest beginning in about 1920. There is little or no order to the material in this collection.
